job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Carlos Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat in Footscray, in Melbourne, with two friends, and my days start with coffee and an AI assistant helping me plan the day. I'm doing a master's in financial analysis, and I spend my spare hours on a free weekly newsletter that explains company reports in plain words. It has about 600 readers and earns me nothing yet, but it's the thing I'm proudest of.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up here?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did an economics bachelor's at RMIT and passed with an average result. No internship, because I was bartending to pay rent and never had a free summer. My dad is a mechanic and my mum works part-time in a school office, so no one can fund me. I owe about 52,000 dollars. I picked financial analysis because I like reading annual reports, which is a weird hobby, and I wanted the newsletter to have more weight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, the tools are useful for chores but nothing more. I'd say it in my newsletter in plain words, and mates would nod, since most already guessed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My situation stays tough, the way it is now. There are about 20 graduate finance jobs in Melbourne that suit me and about 500 applicants, and I have no internship. So the plateau is still a queue, I just have better tools for the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, apply to 25 firms and apply to three or four small advisory shops that might like the newsletter. I'd keep bartending Fridays. And I'd try to turn the newsletter into a paid tier at 5 dollars a month and see if 40 people pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit on edge, but not low. The debt is always there, and I tend to bounce back by building something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a newsletter. Could it turn into money in a world where AI is mostly hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The queue itself. You apply, you get an automated rejection two minutes later, and you wonder if a person read it. After 60 of those it wears you down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the worst part of your situation right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Possibly, in a small way. Even 40 paying readers is 200 dollars a month, which covers a third of my rent, and it proves to employers I can explain finance to real people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the real thing, and the useful response is to learn it fast. I'd write about it in the newsletter and tell people not to wait for permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm reasonably placed, but the entry-level analyst seat is exactly what changes. Pulling numbers, drafting the first memo, checking a model, that's a junior's year. Firms might hire one where they used to hire four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools even more, build two or three public analyses of real companies and put them in the newsletter. I'd apply to funds and advisory shops that like people with a public record. I'd also line up a paid newsletter tier, since a small, direct audience is mine to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit fired up. When things move fast, I'd rather be moving than watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of an analyst's work do you expect software to take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pulling numbers, drafting memos, first-pass models. What stays is deciding which numbers matter and telling a worried investor what to do about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does being good with the tools protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only partly. If everybody has the tools, my skill with them is ordinary. What protects me is a public track record that shows I'm right, or at least thoughtful, over time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest thing in our lifetimes and the sensible response is neither panic nor denial. Governments need to share the gains quickly, and I'd write exactly that, as clearly as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared. If AI does nearly any thinking work, then analysing companies isn't a job anyone has to pay a person for. I'd be 26 with 52,000 of debt, and my best skill would be free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending to the bone, put every dollar on the debt, and look for anything hands-on that lasts the extra three years. My dad's garage might take me on to learn engine diagnostics. I'd keep the newsletter as a hobby, not an income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the kind of feeling where you check the news at 3 a.m. and hate yourself for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents that my dad's trade is safer than my degree for about three years, which is a bitter joke. Then I'd say I'd move into their spare room to stop paying rent, and Mum would pretend not to be glad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the newsletter in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use it to explain what's going on, as honestly as I can. Readers would want a plain voice during chaos, but I couldn't charge for it. Maybe a donation link, and I'd treat it as service.

I'd write that governments should share the gains quickly.
think: Analysing companies might not be a **paid job** any more.
I'd be 26 with **52,000** of debt and my best skill free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the planning window, and I'd tell readers to use it. Learn the tools, build a record, save a bit. I'd keep my tone calm because panic is boring and doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm nervous, but I think it's workable. In five years I could get a first job, clear a good part of the debt, and learn how AI really works inside a firm. I'd be 29 and I'd have options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first analyst job I'm offered and spend two years learning. I'd send 350 dollars a month to the loan, and I'd keep the newsletter going, perhaps with a short course on reading reports. I'd also look for a role in client advice, which is the part machines may be slow to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but in a useful way. It feels like a deadline, and I do well with deadlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you build in five years that you couldn't in two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the work turns into watching software, I'd leave early. If I'm explaining the numbers to a worried client, I'd stay. The test is whether a person still needs to be in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide when to leave finance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A short paid course on reading company reports, aimed at ordinary investors. That's a product I could sell even if machines read the numbers, because people want to understand, not just be told.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can do things properly, so let's do them. I'd write about retraining and fair sharing, and tell readers to learn the tools without drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine, I think. I'd have the debt mostly cleared, a decent job or my own small outfit, and I'd probably be teaching people how to use these tools. At 34 I'd have two or three paths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, get a first job, and put money on the loan. In my spare time I'd keep building the newsletter and the course. I'd go to meetups and spend the decade making a name for being clear and honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty settled, honestly. Some excitement as well. I like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell students starting this degree now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tools, get real experience in the first year, and build something public. The degree is a ticket, not a plan, so don't rely on it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you still fear in the ten-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, but the unfairness bothers me, that a small group could own it all. Ten years is long enough to push for something better, so I'd get involved in the debate.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2-year one, because a free skill and 52,000 in debt is a bad pair. What would help is a plan to share the gains, a debt pause, and honest information early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. I'd miss the moment when a company's annual report finally makes sense and I can explain it to my readers. I'm not sure a machine can feel that.

headlineQuote: I'd miss the moment when a company's annual report finally makes sense and I can explain it to my readers.
portrait: Carlos is a **24-year-old** financial analysis master's student in Melbourne with 52,000 dollars of debt and no internship.
He is **centre** and practical: no villain, a belief in learning fast and sharing the gains.
He is **adaptive**, using AI daily and writing a free newsletter with 600 readers.
His mood runs **anxious** in most worlds, uneasy with a long runway and alarmed at 2028.
His father is a **mechanic**, which becomes his fallback when thinking work is at risk.
biggestWorry: Carlos fears **2028** most, because a free skill and a big debt are a bad pair.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a plan to **share the gains**, a debt pause and early honest information.
